message.content:
A hedgehog's presence, however small, cannot be denied when it breathes within a void of color.

In the lower-left corner of the world, where planes of ochre and cerulean folded into one another, there sat a single living thing: a small hedgehog, its spines catching the light of a sun made of intersecting geometric angles. Upon its nose perched a pair of round spectacles, wire-thin and faintly gold, which had been given to it by some forgotten hand long before the abstract age. It blinked. It breathed. Its small paws pressed against the cool, waxen surface of a broad violet stroke that stretched from horizon to horizon.

The world was not a world but a composition of planes, strokes, and chromatic fields without referential meaning.

There were no trees here, only tall, leaning rectangles of burnt sienna that did not quite touch the sky. There were no rivers, only a long diagonal band of pale blue that suggested water only in the way a word suggests water. The sky was not a sky but a field of thin, overlapping planes—cadet, cerule, a streak of pale rose—each separated from the next by a hair-thin edge of shadow. The horizon was a broad, flat plane of muted gold, and nothing moved within it. The abstractness of it was total: every element existed as shape, as tone, as value. A low, heavy band of umber pressed against the upper register. A tall, leaning form of grey-green stood where a tree might be. There was no meaning behind any of it. The world was a composition, and it was the only world there was.

The spectacles served as a lens through which the hedgehog perceived the composition as something other than emptiness.

Through the thin glass, the hedgehog saw the planes not as blankness but as layers of depth, as planes that receded, as shapes that implied a further world beyond their visible boundary. The long diagonal band of blue became, through the glass, a depth of water, a place where something might dwell. The grey-green form became a trunk, a reach, a reach into something unseen. The hedgehog tilted its small head beneath the round rims, and the world softened, became legible, became a world with a horizon and a ground and something moving within it. It was not the true world, but it was a world it could inhabit, could cross, could cross with its small paws pressing against the cool plane of the ground.

To be the only real thing within an abstract world is to be the only fixed point in a field of pure form.

The hedgehog walked. Its small paws pressed against the broad plane of gold, one, two, three steps, a path of disturbance in the composition. The long diagonal band of blue bent to accommodate its crossing. The tall grey-green form leaned a little further, as if acknowledging the passage of something that was not part of the arrangement. The hedgehog was not a shape in the composition. It was a living thing, a point of reference, a fixed point from which the abstract planes were seen. In the end, it stopped, and the world of planes and tones settled around it, the way a single real note sits within an abstraction of sound. It was the only real thing there was. It blinked. It breathed. Its spines caught the light of the angular sun. The glasses sat on its nose, the only pair in the world.
